conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with a nosebleed that's been going on for a couple of days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago. It stopped for about half a day, but then came back worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You went to another ER where they placed a nasal balloon and found your INR was very high—9, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. They sent me home, but the bleeding didn’t really stop. I kept feeling blood in my throat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we admitted you. Your INR was 9.8 when you arrived here, which is way too high. That means your blood is very thin and not clotting well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I didn’t change anything—no new meds, no extra warfarin. My last INR was 2.7 just a week ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe it’s not due to anything you did. Sometimes INR can rise unexpectedly, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling dizzy the past couple of days. And I had a headache earlier, but it’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That dizziness could be from the blood loss or the high INR. We’ve given you 1 mg of vitamin K by mouth to help reverse the warfarin effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that bring my INR down quickly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps over the next 24 to 48 hours. We’ve also held your warfarin for now. We’ll check your INR again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the nosebleed—what’s next for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted ENT. They’ll see you in the morning to look for the bleeding spot and possibly cauterize it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll numb your nose first. It might be uncomfortable, but not painful. The goal is to stop the bleeding for good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still feel a little blood in the back of my throat, but the nose isn’t actively gushing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. ENT is on their way. Your INR this morning is already coming down to 5.5—vitamin K is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So I’m improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Once we stop the bleeding and your INR is safe, you’ll be on the mend. We’ll restart warfarin when it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, ENT successfully cauterized a small bleeding vessel in your septum using silver nitrate. They also applied a material called Surgicell to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it work? Is the bleeding gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hemostasis was achieved. No more active bleeding. You won’t need nasal packing, so no antibiotics are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds? I take Plavix too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of the bleeding risk, we held both warfarin and Plavix. You’ve missed two doses so far. You’ll hold Plavix for five days total, then restart after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my aspirin? I take baby aspirin every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. Given your history of strokes, we’ve kept you on the baby aspirin the whole time. It’s safer to continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been dizzy—could that be from the nosebleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re monitoring you. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no major blood loss. We’ll keep your meclizine for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest INR is 3.1—much better. Still a bit high, but trending down. We’ll wait until it’s around 2.8 before restarting warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. We’ll check one more INR in the morning. If it’s in range, you can restart warfarin and go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will check your INR three times a week and send the results to our clinic. We’ll adjust your dose if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Thompson. Your INR is now 2.8—perfect. We’ve restarted your warfarin at your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And Plavix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve held it for five days total, including today. You can restart it the day after you go home. We’ll give you written instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No nose picking, avoid blowing your nose hard. Weigh yourself daily—call us if you gain more than 3 pounds, given your heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll discharge you shortly. Take care, and follow up with your primary doctor soon.
